The Bisbee Deportation. Striking miners and random bystanders being loaded into cattle cars for deportation out of the State of Arizona. 1917.

The Bisbee Deportation of 1917 was an illegal vigilante action taken against striking copper workers and the residents of Bisbee, Arizona. It was organized by Phelps Dodge, the major mining company in the area, which provided lists of workers and others who were to be arrested and deported to the local Sheriff.

Cochise County Sheriff Harry Wheeler then deputized 1,200 men as a posse who rounded up 1,186 men, many of whom weren’t on strike or even mine workers. They were loaded at gun point into boxcars, shipped to New Mexico and dropped off without food or water. During the deportation, Phelps Dodge executives seized control of the telegraph and telephones to prevent news of the arrests and expulsion from being reported.

President Wilson ordered U.S. Army troops to assist the men and they were fed and housed in tents and allowed to stay in the camp for two months When ordered to cease these activities by the Arizona Attorney General, and asked what law supported his actions, Sheriff Wheeler answered: "I have no statute that I had in mind. Perhaps everything that I did wasn't legal....It became a question of 'Are you American, or are you not?'"

A federal commission was set up to investigate and found that the deportation was wholly illegal. However, Arizona officials never initiated criminal proceedings against those responsible. Some people filed civil suits, but in the first case the jury determined that the deportations represented good public policy and refused to grant relief.

It makes sense in my mind that the password requirements are so out of the normal way of thinking that most people can't remember them all and therefore reuse portions of passwords or simply make small changes when going from one service to the next.

They say it is for security sake but I've heard that passwords that just involve 3 randomized words are harder to decode than something like Pword$42.

By giving us restrictions on how to make the passwords aren't they also making it easier to dial into them and figure them out?

Granted you can of course make your password much longer and Pwordispussypony#420, though I've seen character limits.

What are your thoughts?
Do you think password requirements are set in order to make it easier to crack them?
No. Password restrictions are there to make cracking harder. Some sysadmins just lack creativity.

Unfortunately, people don't know how to properly implement rules, so it usually just gets limited to at least 1 of each character type and at least 'x' characters long. And some websites actually have a small (10-16) upper-bound on the length of the password too for no good reason. What I've started doing lately is combining the two (at least 1 letter, number, and symbol) along with randomized words, and just kinda do both.

I never thought about that.

On one hand, requiring multiple character class increases the number of combinations to test, which increase the time it takes to brute force a password. Same with the length. Forbidding dictionary words prevent "shortcuts".

On the other hand, since the passwords are harder to remember, some people will tend to reuse the password everywhere. Also, some may, when prompted to change the password, be lazy and just change a single character. This pokes a big hole into the security of a system.

So, where do those policies come from? It is reasonable to think that it is just a recommendation from programmers who didn't think about the human aspect, but it is also possible that it could be a sneaky way to poke holes into systems / networks under the guise of increase of security.
